pos: n. phrase (Latin: God's absolute power; what He can do, considered apart from what He has actually willed to do)
etymology: Latin potentia, power, + absoluta, loosed, considered in itself. The scholastics paired it with potentia ordinata, the power God has bound to the order He has actually decreed. The distinction is not two gods. It is one God, speaking of what He is able to do and of what He has pledged to do.
biblical_def: Potentia absoluta names what God can do, considered in itself. Gabriel said it to Mary: “For with God nothing shall be impossible” (Luk 1:37). Job had already said it of the counsel: “I know that thou canst do every thing, and that no thought can be withholden from thee” (Job 42:2). The psalmist puts the same fact in the heavens: “But our God is in the heavens: he hath done whatsoever he hath pleased” (Psa 115:3). And the Lord names the bound: “With men this is impossible; but with God all things are possible” (Mat 19:26). The distinction is pastoral as well as scholastic. God is not limited by the creature. He is limited only by Himself: “he cannot deny himself” (2Ti 2:13). Absolute power is not a license for God to become another God. It is the confession that what He has not done, He still could have done, and that what He has sworn, He will not unsay.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for the Latin pair. Potentia absoluta is scholastic shorthand for God's power considered in itself, as distinct from the order He has actually willed.
webster_full: POTENTIA ABSOLUTA, Latin, absolute power. Scholastic theological phrase, not an 1828 English headword.
What God can do, considered apart from the covenant and the decree He has actually made.
Paired with potentia ordinata: the same power, now bound to the order God has freely set.
Does not mean God can lie, sin, or deny Himself. Absolute is not arbitrary.
scriptures: Luk 1:37
For with God nothing shall be impossible.
Job 42:2
I know that thou canst do every thing, and that no thought can be withholden from thee.
But our God is in the heavens: he hath done whatsoever he hath pleased.
But Jesus beheld them, and said unto them, With men this is impossible; but with God all things are possible.
If we believe not, yet he abideth faithful: he cannot deny himself.
corruption_summary: Absolute power is turned into a God who might unsay Himself, and the Bible's God cannot deny Himself.
corruption_paragraphs: The distinction is corrupted in two opposite directions. The first makes potentia absoluta a God behind God — a bare will that might, on another day, save without Christ, damn the elect, or unsay a promise. That is not the God of 2 Timothy 2:13. He cannot deny Himself. The power is absolute as to the creature; it is not lawless as to the divine nature. A theology that uses the phrase to make the gospel a disposable option has already left the schools for speculation.

The second direction denies the distinction altogether and treats the present order as if God could have done nothing else. Job 42:2 will not wear that either. Thou canst do every thing. The counsel He has taken is free. He was not forced into this world, this covenant, this cross. He chose them. That is why worship is not resignation to necessity. It is thanks for a will that did not have to be kind and was.

Psalm 115:3 belongs in both halves. He hath done whatsoever He hath pleased — that is ordained power, the will executed. And the pleasure is His, not extracted from the creature. The man who needs God to have been unable to do otherwise has not yet learned to call grace grace.
roots_summary: Latin potentia absoluta; Greek dunatos (G1415), possible, able; Hebrew yakol (H3201), to be able.
roots_lines: Latin potentia absoluta — power considered in itself; paired in the schools with potentia ordinata.
Greek adunateo (G101) — to be impossible; Luke 1:37, nothing shall be impossible.
Hebrew yakol (H3201) — to be able; Job 42:2, thou canst do every thing.
usage: “With God nothing shall be impossible” — said of a conception, not of a contradiction.
“Thou canst do every thing” — and no thought withholden.
“He cannot deny himself” — absolute is not lawless.

pos: n. phrase (Latin: God's ordained power; what He has actually willed and bound Himself to do in this world)
etymology: Latin ordinata, set in order, from ordo. The same power as absoluta, now considered as God has actually arranged the world, the covenant, and the means. Not a second power. A second way of speaking of one power.
biblical_def: Potentia ordinata is the power God has actually put to work. He does not merely possess might. He has taken counsel and will perform it: “My counsel shall stand, and I will do all my pleasure” (Isa 46:10). He has sworn and will not repent: “The Lord hath sworn, and will not repent, Thou art a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek” (Psa 110:4). The gospel itself is an ordained thing: “Him, being delivered by the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God, ye have taken, and by wicked hands have crucified and slain” (Act 2:23). And the blessing is not a mood. It is a word God will not unsay: “For men verily swear by the greater: and an oath for confirmation is to them an end of all strife. Wherein God, willing more abundantly to shew unto the heirs of promise the immutability of his counsel, confirmed it by an oath” (Heb 6:16–17). The ordained power is why a sinner may rest. God has not left Himself loose options against His own promise.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for the Latin pair. Potentia ordinata is the scholastic name for God's power as He has actually bound it to the decree, the covenant, and the sworn word.
webster_full: POTENTIA ORDINATA, Latin, ordained power. Scholastic theological phrase, not an 1828 English headword.
God's power considered as He has actually willed this world, this covenant, these means.
Not a weaker power than the absolute. The same power, now pledged.
The ground of assurance: what God has sworn, He will perform.
scriptures: Declaring the end from the beginning, and from ancient times the things that are not yet done, saying, My counsel shall stand, and I will do all my pleasure:
The LORD hath sworn, and will not repent, Thou art a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek.
Act 2:23
Him, being delivered by the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God, ye have taken, and by wicked hands have crucified and slain:
Heb 6:17
Wherein God, willing more abundantly to shew unto the heirs of promise the immutability of his counsel, confirmed it by an oath:
But our God is in the heavens: he hath done whatsoever he hath pleased.
corruption_summary: Ordained power is treated as a cage God is stuck in, and Scripture treats it as a counsel He freely bound with an oath.
corruption_paragraphs: Process theology and its softer cousins hear “ordained” as if God had been overtaken by the world He made and must now cope. Isaiah 46:10 is the opposite sentence. My counsel shall stand. I will do all my pleasure. The order is His pleasure executed, not His defeat managed. A God who is learning the plot with us is not the God who delivered the Son by determinate counsel.

The other corruption is pastoral despair dressed as humility: perhaps God has reserved a private will against the promise, and the gospel is what He says in public. Hebrews 6 was written to kill that thought. He confirmed the counsel by an oath, that by two immutable things we might have strong consolation. The ordained power is not a threat behind the offer. It is the offer made unbreakable.

Acts 2:23 holds the pair the schools were trying to name. Determinate counsel and wicked hands in one verse. God ordained the cross. Men meant it for evil. The ordained power does not excuse the hands. It does mean the hands did not surprise Him.
roots_summary: Latin potentia ordinata; Hebrew etsah (H6098), counsel; Greek boule (G1012), counsel, purpose.
roots_lines: Latin potentia ordinata — power as bound to the order God has set.
Hebrew etsah (H6098) — counsel; Isaiah 46:10, my counsel shall stand.
Greek boule (G1012) — counsel; Acts 2:23, determinate counsel; Hebrews 6:17, immutability of his counsel.
usage: “My counsel shall stand” — ordained is not trapped.
“Confirmed it by an oath” — so the heirs would stop guessing.
“Determinate counsel” — and wicked hands in the same sentence.

pos: n. phrase (the Dominican account of how God applies the second cause to its act, moving the will before it moves)
etymology: Latin praemotio physica: prae, before, + motio, a moving, + physica, real rather than merely moral. Domingo Bañez and the Dominican school used it against Molina's middle knowledge. God does not wait to see what the will would do. He applies the will to its act.
biblical_def: Physical premotion is a school's name for a biblical fact: God does not merely invite the will. He works it. “For it is God which worketh in you both to will and to do of his good pleasure” (Php 2:13). Solomon had already said the king's heart is in that hand: “The king's heart is in the hand of the Lord, as the rivers of water: he turneth it whithersoever he will” (Pro 21:1). The prepared will is His work: “Lord, thou wilt ordain peace for us: for thou also hast wrought all our works in us” (Isa 26:12). And the steps are not self-started: “The steps of a good man are ordered by the Lord” (Psa 37:23). Jeremiah puts the inability without that motion in one clause: “O Lord, I know that the way of man is not in himself: it is not in man that walketh to direct his steps” (Jer 10:23). The dictionary does not baptize every Dominican inference. It will not surrender the verses to a God who only persuades.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for the Latin phrase. Physical premotion is the Dominican name for God's real application of the creaturely will to its act, prior to the act.
webster_full: PHYSICAL PREMOTION, from Latin praemotio physica. Scholastic phrase, not an 1828 English headword.
God's motion of the second cause to its act, real (physical) rather than merely suasive (moral).
Bañezian answer to Molina: God does not depend on a middle knowledge of what the will would do.
The biblical cargo is Philippians 2:13: He worketh in you both to will and to do.
scriptures: Php 2:13
For it is God which worketh in you both to will and to do of his good pleasure.
Pro 21:1
The king's heart is in the hand of the LORD, as the rivers of water: he turneth it whithersoever he will.
LORD, thou wilt ordain peace for us: for thou also hast wrought all our works in us.
The steps of a good man are ordered by the LORD: and he delighteth in his way.
O LORD, I know that the way of man is not in himself: it is not in man that walketh to direct his steps.
corruption_summary: Premotion is either denied so that God only persuades, or inflated so that the sinner is a stick God waves, and Scripture holds both the work and the will.
corruption_paragraphs: Molina's middle knowledge was built to keep God sovereign without letting Him apply the will. God looks down the tree of what free creatures would do and chooses a world. Physical premotion is the Dominican refusal of that glance. Proverbs 21:1 does not say the Lord consults the river. He turneth it. A theology that cannot say that of the king's heart will not say it of the sinner's, and then Philippians 2:13 has to be read as courtesy.

The opposite error is the one the Jesuits accused the Dominicans of, and sometimes earned: a God who moves the will the way a man moves a stone, so that the sinner is not a second cause at all. Jeremiah 10:23 is not that. It is not in man that walketh to direct his steps — the walker is still a walker. The Reformed concursus is safer speech than some Bañezian pages: God works in the will as a will, not instead of one.

Isaiah 26:12 is the confession the argument is about. Thou hast wrought all our works in us. A congregation that can say that without embarrassment has already left both Molinism and fatalism. The work is His. The works are ours. The pleasure is His good pleasure.
roots_summary: Latin praemotio physica; Greek energeo (G1754), to work in; Hebrew natan / turning of the heart.
roots_lines: Latin praemotio physica — a real premotion of the second cause; Bañez against Molina.
Greek energeo (G1754) — to work, be operative; Philippians 2:13, worketh in you both to will and to do.
Hebrew image: the heart as watercourses; Proverbs 21:1, He turneth it whithersoever He will.
usage: “Worketh in you both to will and to do” — not merely to advise.
“He turneth it whithersoever he will” — said of a king's heart.
“It is not in man that walketh” — the walker is still a walker.

pos: n. (the claim that a word, especially being, is said of God and the creature in one sense)
etymology: Latin univocus, of one voice, from unus + vox. Scotus argued that being is said of God and creatures univocally, or we cannot talk of God at all. The Reformed analogical tradition answered that the word is neither the same nor a mere pun. It is analogical.
biblical_def: Univocity is a claim about speech: that when we say God is, we mean the same thing we mean when we say a man is. Scripture will not give us that ease, and it will not give us silence. “To whom then will ye liken God? or what likeness will ye compare unto him?” (Isa 40:18). Moses had already heard the Name that refuses a genus: “I AM THAT I AM” (Exo 3:14). The seraphim do not say He is being. They say He is holy: “Holy, holy, holy, is the Lord of hosts” (Isa 6:3). And yet the same Bible talks constantly, because God has talked first: “God, who at sundry times and in divers manners spake in time past unto the fathers by the prophets” (Heb 1:1). The creature's words hold because He stoops, not because being is a shared floor. Paul names the gap and the gift together: “For who hath known the mind of the Lord? or who hath been his counsellor?” (Rom 11:34).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines univocal as having one meaning only, and univocation as the agreement of several things in one name or one meaning. The theological fight is whether being is such a name for God and the creature.
webster_full: UNIVOCAL, a. [L. unus, one, and vox, word.]
Having one meaning only. A univocal word is opposed to an equivocal, which has two or more significations.
UNIVOCATION, n. Agreement of name and meaning.
In the schools the question is whether being is univocal of God and creatures.
scriptures: To whom then will ye liken God? or what likeness will ye compare unto him?
Exo 3:14
And God said unto Moses, I AM THAT I AM: and he said, Thus shalt thou say unto the children of Israel, I AM hath sent me unto you.
Isa 6:3
And one cried unto another, and said, Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts: the whole earth is full of his glory.
Heb 1:1
God, who at sundry times and in divers manners spake in time past unto the fathers by the prophets,
For who hath known the mind of the Lord? or who hath been his counsellor?
corruption_summary: Univocity either flattens God into the largest being in the room, or its denial is used to say we cannot speak of Him at all.
corruption_paragraphs: Scotus feared that if being is not univocal, theology is a set of honours paid to an unknown. Isaiah 40:18 is the fear's other side: if the likeness is easy, we have made an idol. The analogical way is not a shrug. It is the confession that our words work because God has named Himself, and they do not work as if He were one more item in the inventory. I AM THAT I AM is not a shared category. It is a Name.

The modern version of univocity is cruder. God becomes the biggest person, the nicest boss, the sky-father whose love is our love scaled up. Holy, holy, holy is not a volume knob. A pulpit that can only say God is like us, more so, has already lost the seraphim.

The opposite corruption uses analogy as a gag. If our words do not mean the same, they mean nothing, and then Hebrews 1:1 is a problem. God spoke. The dictionary will not surrender speech to keep God strange, and it will not surrender strangeness to keep speech easy. Analogia fidei is already on the shelf. Univocity is the claim that shelf was never needed.
roots_summary: Latin univocus, one voice; Hebrew damah (H1819), to liken; Greek homoios is not the point — the Name is.
roots_lines: Latin univocus — of one voice; opposed to aequivocus and to analogical predication.
Hebrew damah (H1819) — to liken, compare; Isaiah 40:18, to whom will ye liken God.
Hebrew ehyeh asher ehyeh — I AM THAT I AM; Exodus 3:14, the Name that will not sit in a genus.
usage: “To whom then will ye liken God” — the question that ends easy being.
“I AM THAT I AM” — not a shared floor.
“Holy, holy, holy” — not our goodness turned up.

pos: n. (the claim that a word is said of God and the creature in wholly different senses, so that the shared sound is a pun)
etymology: Latin aequivocus, of equal voice and unequal meaning, from aequus + vox. If univocity makes God a being among beings, equivocity makes every predicate a homonym. The analogical middle is the dictionary's path because Scripture talks and forbids likeness in the same breath.
biblical_def: Equivocity is the claim that our words about God share only a sound with our words about the world. Scripture refuses both the flattening and the gag. Moses is told the secret things belong to the Lord, and the revealed things belong to us: “The secret things belong unto the Lord our God: but those things which are revealed belong unto us and to our children for ever” (Deu 29:29). God speaks so as to be understood: “I have not spoken in secret, in a dark place of the earth” (Isa 45:19). And yet no man has seen Him: “No man hath seen God at any time” (John 1:18). Paul does not conclude silence. He concludes gift: “the things of God knoweth no man, but the Spirit of God. Now we have received, not the spirit of the world, but the spirit which is of God; that we might know the things that are freely given to us of God” (1Co 2:11–12). Equivocity would make that reception a noise. The Spirit makes it knowledge.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines equivocal as being of doubtful signification, and equivocation as the use of words of doubtful meaning. In the schools, equivocity is the claim that God-talk and creature-talk share a sound only.
webster_full: EQUIVOCAL, a. [L. aequivocus; aequus, equal, and vox, word.]
Being of doubtful signification; that may be understood in different senses.
EQUIVOCATION, n. Ambiguity of speech; the use of words or expressions that are susceptible of a double signification.
Theological equivocity is stronger: the claim that the shared word is a mere homonym when said of God.
scriptures: The secret things belong unto the LORD our God: but those things which are revealed belong unto us and to our children for ever, that we may do all the words of this law.
I have not spoken in secret, in a dark place of the earth: I said not unto the seed of Jacob, Seek ye me in vain: I the LORD speak righteousness, I declare things that are right.
John 1:18
No man hath seen God at any time; the only begotten Son, which is in the bosom of the Father, he hath declared him.
For what man knoweth the things of a man, save the spirit of man which is in him? even so the things of God knoweth no man, but the Spirit of God.
Now we have received, not the spirit of the world, but the spirit which is of God; that we might know the things that are freely given to us of God.
corruption_summary: Equivocity is used to keep God ineffable by making revelation a shrug, and Deuteronomy 29:29 already divided the secret from the revealed.
corruption_paragraphs: A certain apophatic fashion treats every predicate as an honour paid to silence. Isaiah 45:19 will not have it. I have not spoken in secret. The God of Israel is not the unknown god. He has talked in the open, and the talking is for keeping, not for guessing.

Deuteronomy 29:29 is the map the schools keep redrawing. Secret things belong unto the Lord. Revealed things belong unto us and to our children. Equivocity collapses the second column into the first. Then the confession becomes a mood, and the children inherit a hush.

First Corinthians 2 is why the dictionary will not take the gag. No man knows the things of God, but the Spirit of God, and we have received the Spirit that we might know what is freely given. Knowledge is gift, not univocal climb and not equivocal shrug. Analogia fidei is the name of that gift when it is reading Scripture by Scripture.
roots_summary: Latin aequivocus; Hebrew sathar (H5641), to hide, secret things; Greek apokalupto (G601), to reveal.
roots_lines: Latin aequivocus — equal voice, unequal sense; the homonym claim.
Hebrew nistaroth (H5641) — secret things; Deuteronomy 29:29, they belong unto the Lord.
Greek ginosko (G1097) — to know; 1 Corinthians 2:12, that we might know the things freely given.
usage: “Those things which are revealed belong unto us” — not a shrug.
“I have not spoken in secret” — the opposite of equivocal theology.
“That we might know” — gift, not a pun.

pos: n. phrase (Latin: the Trinity's works toward the creature, which are undivided)
etymology: Latin opera, works, + ad extra, toward what is outside. The schools distinguished these from opera ad intra, the personal works that stay within the Godhead (generation, spiration). Outward, the three Persons work one work. Inward, the relations of origin remain distinct.
biblical_def: Opera ad extra are the works God does toward the world, and they are not split among the Persons as if creation were the Father's hobby and redemption the Son's. “In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth” (Gen 1:1), and the Spirit was there: “And the Spirit of God moved upon the face of the waters” (Gen 1:2), and the Word was there: “All things were made by him; and without him was not any thing made that was made” (John 1:3). Paul will not let the church assign the works to separate gods: “But to us there is but one God, the Father, of whom are all things, and we in him; and one Lord Jesus Christ, by whom are all things, and we by him” (1Co 8:6). The same undivided work is in the raising: “But if the Spirit of him that raised up Jesus from the dead dwell in you, he that raised up Christ from the dead shall also quicken your mortal bodies by his Spirit that dwelleth in you” (Rom 8:11). One God. Three Persons. One work outward.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for the Latin phrase. Opera ad extra names the Trinity's outward works, which are undivided, as distinct from the inward personal properties.
webster_full: OPERA AD EXTRA, Latin, works toward the outside. Scholastic Trinitarian phrase, not an 1828 English headword.
Creation, providence, incarnation, redemption, judgment: one work of the one God.
The Persons are not three agents splitting a job. Appropriations name how Scripture often speaks; they do not divide the essence.
Paired with opera ad intra: generation and spiration remain personal and inward.
scriptures: Gen 1:1
In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth.
Gen 1:2
And the earth was without form, and void; and darkness was upon the face of the deep. And the Spirit of God moved upon the face of the waters.
John 1:3
All things were made by him; and without him was not any thing made that was made.
But to us there is but one God, the Father, of whom are all things, and we in him; and one Lord Jesus Christ, by whom are all things, and we by him.
Rom 8:11
But if the Spirit of him that raised up Jesus from the dead dwell in you, he that raised up Christ from the dead shall also quicken your mortal bodies by his Spirit that dwelleth in you.
corruption_summary: The outward works are either split into three jobs or collapsed so that the Persons are only masks, and Scripture will have neither.
corruption_paragraphs: A crude tritheism assigns creation to the Father, the cross to the Son, and Pentecost to the Spirit, as if the Godhead were a committee. Genesis 1 will not start that way, and John 1 will not let the Word be a subcontractor. All things were made by Him. First Corinthians 8:6 holds of whom and by whom in one confession, not two deities.

The modalist opposite hears undivided and concludes the Persons are costumes. Romans 8:11 names the Father who raised, the Son who was raised, and the Spirit who dwells and quickens, without splitting the work or erasing the names. Undivided is not unnamed.

Appropriations are a help when they stay humble. We say the Father creates, the Son redeems, the Spirit sanctifies, because Scripture often talks that way. We do not then write a fourth god called the Committee. The dictionary's Trinity is the one who made the world and raised the Son by the Spirit, and still is Father, Son, and Holy Ghost.
roots_summary: Latin opera ad extra; Hebrew bara (H1254), create; Greek ginomai (G1096) in John 1:3, were made.
roots_lines: Latin opera ad extra — outward works of the Trinity; undivided.
Hebrew bara (H1254) — create; Genesis 1:1, God created.
Greek egeneto (G1096) — were made; John 1:3, all things by the Word.
usage: “The Spirit of God moved” — already in the second verse.
“All things were made by him” — the Word is not a subcontractor.
“Of whom … by whom” — one confession, not two gods.

pos: n. phrase (Latin: the Trinity's inward personal works — the Son's generation, the Spirit's spiration)
etymology: Latin ad intra, toward the inside. These works do not terminate on the creature. They are the relations of origin by which the Persons are distinct: the Father begets, the Son is begotten, the Spirit proceeds. Outward works are common. These are not.
biblical_def: Opera ad intra are the works that stay within the Godhead. The Son is begotten, not made: “For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son” (John 3:16). The Father's voice names that relation in history because it is true in eternity: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Mat 3:17). The Spirit's coming-forth is not an afterthought of Pentecost. It is from the Father, sent by the Son: “But when the Comforter is come, whom I will send unto you from the Father, even the Spirit of truth, which proceedeth from the Father, he shall testify of me” (John 15:26). Proverbs had already spoken in the Son's voice of being brought forth before the hills: “When there were no depths, I was brought forth” (Pro 8:24). And the benediction keeps the three without blending them: “The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Ghost, be with you all” (2Co 13:14). Inward works are why the names are not labels we invented for moods.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for the Latin phrase. Opera ad intra names the personal works of origin in the Trinity, as distinct from the undivided outward works.
webster_full: OPERA AD INTRA, Latin, works toward the inside. Scholastic Trinitarian phrase, not an 1828 English headword.
Eternal generation of the Son; eternal procession of the Spirit.
These works do not terminate on the creature. They are how the Persons are distinct.
The outward works are common to the three; these are not shared as works, though the essence is one.
scriptures: John 3:16
For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life.
Mat 3:17
And lo a voice from heaven, saying, This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.
John 15:26
But when the Comforter is come, whom I will send unto you from the Father, even the Spirit of truth, which proceedeth from the Father, he shall testify of me:
Pro 8:24
When there were no depths, I was brought forth; when there were no fountains abounding with water.
The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Ghost, be with you all. Amen.
corruption_summary: Inward works are treated as metaphors for missions, or as a fourth thing behind the Persons, and the Bible's names are real.
corruption_paragraphs: A tired modern habit says begotten only means the birth at Bethlehem, and proceedeth only means Pentecost. John 15:26 will not be reduced to a calendar. The Spirit proceedeth from the Father, and the Son sends Him. That is a relation told in time because it is true before time. Eternal procession is already on this shelf. Opera ad intra is the family name for that class of works.

The other error invents a divine essence that begets and proceeds as a fourth actor, so that the Father is a mask the essence wears. Matthew 3:17 is a voice, and it says my Son. The Persons are not offices of a nameless stuff. The inward works are personal.

Second Corinthians 13:14 is how the church talks when it has not forgotten the inward works. Grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, love of God, communion of the Holy Ghost. Three names. One blessing. No committee, no costume-change, no leftover god behind them.
roots_summary: Latin opera ad intra; Greek monogenes (G3439), only begotten; ekporeuomai (G1607), to proceed.
roots_lines: Latin opera ad intra — inward personal works of the Trinity.
Greek monogenes (G3439) — only begotten; John 3:16, 1:18, 1 John 4:9.
Greek ekporeuomai (G1607) — to proceed; John 15:26, which proceedeth from the Father.
usage: “His only begotten Son” — not a metaphor for a mission.
“Which proceedeth from the Father” — said before Pentecost is finished.
“The communion of the Holy Ghost” — a name, not a mood.

pos: n. (the claim that the divine nature itself suffered; or, loosely, any speech that makes God passible in His deity)
etymology: Greek theos, God, + pascho, to suffer. The fifth-century Theopaschite formula, “one of the Trinity suffered in the flesh,” is orthodox when it means the Person. It is heresy when it means the divine nature underwent change, pain, or death.
biblical_def: Theopaschitism is the error of putting suffering in the wrong place. Scripture puts it in the Person, in the flesh. Paul can say the church was purchased “with his own blood” (Act 20:28), and that they “crucified the Lord of glory” (1Co 2:8), because the one Person who is God has a human nature that bleeds. Peter says the same without moving the pain into the Godhead as Godhead: “For Christ also hath once suffered for sins, the just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God, being put to death in the flesh” (1Pe 3:18). The Word was made flesh (John 1:14), and it is that flesh the nails found. Hebrews keeps the priest human enough to suffer and divine enough to save: “For we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities; but was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin” (Heb 4:15). The Person suffered. The divine nature did not become mortal.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for the term. Theopaschitism names the error of ascribing suffering to the divine nature, as distinct from the orthodox predication of suffering to the one Person in the flesh.
webster_full: THEOPASCHITISM, from Greek theos + pascho. Patristic and scholastic term, not an 1828 English headword.
Heresy: the divine nature suffered, changed, or died.
Orthodox near-formula: one of the Trinity suffered in the flesh — the Person, not the deity as deity.
Guarded by impassibility and by the communicatio idiomatum rightly limited.
scriptures: Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood.
Which none of the princes of this world knew: for had they known it, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory.
For Christ also hath once suffered for sins, the just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God, being put to death in the flesh, but quickened by the Spirit:
John 1:14
And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth.
Heb 4:15
For we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities; but was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin.
corruption_summary: Either God is made to suffer as God, so that the Redeemer needs a redeemer, or the cross is kept so far from God that the Lord of glory was not crucified.
corruption_paragraphs: Process theism and a good deal of modern preaching want a God who suffers in His deity, because a God who cannot suffer is thought not to love. First Peter 3:18 already has the love, and it locates the death: put to death in the flesh. A passible divine nature is a nature that can be damaged. Then the cross is not God saving. It is God breaking, and there is no one left above the wreck to raise Him.

The opposite error is so frightened of theopaschitism that it will not let Paul say the Lord of glory was crucified. First Corinthians 2:8 is the communicatio, not the heresy. The title is divine. The crucifixion is of the Person. Acts 20:28 is blood that is His own. The dictionary already has the grammar on the communicatio page. This page names the ditch on the other side of that road.

Hebrews 4:15 is why the church may not pick the ditch. We have a priest who can be touched, and we have a God who does not come undone. The feeling of our infirmities is the flesh assumed, not the essence revised. Impassibility is not coldness. It is why the suffering of the Son is a gift and not a divine emergency.
roots_summary: Greek theos (G2316) + pascho (G3958); Latin formula unus de Trinitate passus est carne.
roots_lines: Greek pascho (G3958) — to suffer; 1 Peter 3:18, Christ hath once suffered; Hebrews 4:15, touched with the feeling.
Greek sarx (G4561) — flesh; John 1:14, the Word was made flesh; 1 Peter 3:18, put to death in the flesh.
Latin unus de Trinitate passus est carne — orthodox if it means the Person in the flesh.
usage: “Purchased with his own blood” — the Person, not a damaged deity.
“Crucified the Lord of glory” — communicatio, not theopaschitism.
“Put to death in the flesh” — Peter already located it.

pos: n. phrase (Latin: God's knowledge of vision; His knowledge of what He has actually decreed, as distinct from mere possibles and from Molina's middle knowledge)
etymology: Latin scientia, knowledge, + visionis, of vision. The older school named three: knowledge of simple intelligence (what is possible), knowledge of vision (what is and will be, because decreed), and, with Molina, a middle knowledge of what free creatures would do. The Reformed keep the first two and refuse the third as a God who looks before He wills.
biblical_def: Scientia visionis is God's knowledge of the world He has actually willed, not a catalog of unused options. Isaiah's God declares the end from the beginning: “Declaring the end from the beginning, and from ancient times the things that are not yet done, saying, My counsel shall stand, and I will do all my pleasure” (Isa 46:10). Known unto Him are all His works: “Known unto God are all his works from the beginning of the world” (Act 15:18). The darkness is not dark to Him: “Yea, the darkness hideth not from thee; but the night shineth as the day” (Psa 139:12). And the word is not a guess about what we might do. It is the word that makes: “The Lord of hosts hath sworn, saying, Surely as I have thought, so shall it come to pass” (Isa 14:24). Hebrews puts the finished view in one clause: “Neither is there any creature that is not manifest in his sight: but all things are naked and opened unto the eyes of him with whom we have to do” (Heb 4:13). Vision here is not eyesight. It is the knowledge of what is, because He willed it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for the Latin phrase. Scientia visionis is the scholastic name for God's knowledge of actuals, as distinct from possibles and from middle knowledge.
webster_full: SCIENTIA VISIONIS, Latin, knowledge of vision. Scholastic phrase, not an 1828 English headword.
God's knowledge of what is, has been, and will be, because He has decreed it.
Distinct from scientia simplicis intelligentiae (possibles) and from Molina's scientia media.
The biblical cargo is Acts 15:18 and Isaiah 46:10: known works, declared end, standing counsel.
scriptures: Declaring the end from the beginning, and from ancient times the things that are not yet done, saying, My counsel shall stand, and I will do all my pleasure:
Known unto God are all his works from the beginning of the world.
Yea, the darkness hideth not from thee; but the night shineth as the day: the darkness and the light are both alike to thee.
The LORD of hosts hath sworn, saying, Surely as I have thought, so shall it come to pass; and as I have purposed, so shall it stand:
Heb 4:13
Neither is there any creature that is not manifest in his sight: but all things are naked and opened unto the eyes of him with whom we have to do.
corruption_summary: Vision-knowledge is either reduced to a forecast of our freedom, or inflated into a stare that never decides, and Isaiah's God declares because He will do.
corruption_paragraphs: Molina's middle knowledge sits between possibles and actuals and claims to know what the creature would do if placed. The dictionary already answered that on the middle-knowledge page. Scientia visionis is the older name for the knowledge that does not wait on that would. Isaiah 46:10 joins declaring and doing in one breath. The end is declared because the pleasure will be done.

Open theism hears vision and thinks God is watching a game He did not script. Acts 15:18 is not sports commentary. Known unto God are all His works from the beginning of the world. The works are His. The knowing is not a later report.

Hebrews 4:13 is why the phrase still matters in a pulpit. All things are naked and opened unto the eyes of Him with whom we have to do. That is not a threat that God might be surprised by a better story. It is the comfort that nothing in the story is off His book, and the warning that nothing in the story is off His book.
roots_summary: Latin scientia visionis; Hebrew nagad (H5046), to declare; Greek gnostos (G1110), known.
roots_lines: Latin scientia visionis — knowledge of actuals; not middle knowledge.
Hebrew nagad (H5046) — to declare; Isaiah 46:10, declaring the end from the beginning.
Greek gnostos (G1110) — known; Acts 15:18, known unto God are all his works.
usage: “Declaring the end from the beginning” — vision, not a forecast.
“Known unto God are all his works” — His works, from the beginning.
“Naked and opened unto the eyes” — with whom we have to do.

pos: n. & adj. (the fourth-century party that said the Son is like the Father while refusing both homoousios and homoiousios)
etymology: Greek homoios, like, similar. The Homoians, gathered around Acacius of Caesarea and the Dated Creed (359), would say only that the Son is like the Father, and forbade ousia-language as unscriptural. It is not the Homoiousian “like in substance.” It is likeness with the substance question tabled, which is how Arianism learned to sound modest.
biblical_def: A Homoian will give you likeness and withhold the thing. Scripture will not make that trade. The Son is not merely like God. He is the image: “Who is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature” (Col 1:15). He is the express image: “Who being the brightness of his glory, and the express image of his person” (Heb 1:3). He is in the form of God and thought it not robbery to be equal: “Who, being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God” (Php 2:6). John does not say like. He says was: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1). And the Jews understood the claim: “Therefore the Jews sought the more to kill him, because he not only had broken the sabbath, but said also that God was his Father, making himself equal with God” (John 5:18). Likeness-language that forbids equality-language has already chosen a side.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for the party name. Homoian names the fourth-century creed that would say the Son is like the Father and would not say of one substance.
webster_full: HOMOIAN, from Greek homoios, like. Patristic party name, not an 1828 English headword.
The Dated Creed (359) and Acacius: the Son is like the Father, as the Scriptures say; ousia-terms forbidden.
Distinct from homoousios (same substance) and homoiousios (like in substance).
Arianism in a modest voice: likeness without the substance question.
scriptures: Col 1:15
Who is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature:
Heb 1:3

Who being the brightness of his glory, and the express image of his person, and upholding all things by the word of his power, when he had by himself purged our sins, sat down on the right hand of the Majesty on high;
Php 2:6
Who, being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God:
John 1:1
In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.
John 5:18
Therefore the Jews sought the more to kill him, because he not only had broken the sabbath, but said also that God was his Father, making himself equal with God.
corruption_summary: Likeness is offered as peace, and the New Testament's words are image, express image, equal, and was God.
corruption_paragraphs: The Dated Creed sounded irenic. Why fight about a word the Bible does not use, when we can all say the Son is like the Father? Hebrews 1:3 is why. Express image of His person is not a simile. It is identity of glory in a distinct Person. A peace that tables ousia has not made peace. It has hidden the question the Jews already heard in John 5:18.

Modern versions of the same move are everywhere. Jesus is godlike, Christlike, a window onto the divine, the best picture we have. Colossians 1:15 will not stay at picture. He is the image of the invisible God, and the next verses give Him creation and the fullness. A pulpit that will only say like has taken Acacius's bargain without the Greek.

Philippians 2:6 is the word the Homoians could not keep. Equal with God, not robbery. The confession of Nicaea did not invent that. It refused to let likeness talk bury it. Homoousios is already on this shelf. Homoian is the party that asked us to live without it and call the loss humility.
roots_summary: Greek homoios, like; contrasted with homoousios (G3673 family) and eikon (G1504), image.
roots_lines: Greek homoios — like, similar; the Homoian ceiling.
Greek eikon (G1504) — image; Colossians 1:15, the image of the invisible God.
Greek charakter (G5481) — express image; Hebrews 1:3 only in this sense of the Son.
usage: “The express image of his person” — not a simile.
“Thought it not robbery to be equal” — the word Homoians tabled.
“The Word was God” — John did not say like.
